Made by and Forwarded by C.D.I. H.Grubb.
In connection with the arrest of thirty-one
communists on behalf of the Chinese Authorities by the
Municipal Police between July 22 and 27, 1935, the question
of recommendations for awards for those participating has been
duly considered. Although the results, from a political point
of view, were exceptionally good, nothing really outstanding
and deserving of special commendation was performed, apart
from a great deal of hard work involved, the brunt of which
fell on the staff of S.2.
In the first instance the information leading to
the initial arrests was furnished by the Bureau of Public
Safety and further arrests resulted from evidence secured in
the course of the various raids.

Summary of Evidence.

Herein is contained a summary of evidence obtained to date against 31 persons arrested between July 22, and July 27, 1935 on warrants issued at the request of the Bureau of Public Safety, charging these persons with being communists.

Serial Nos. 1 to 11 held at Gordon Road Station.

Serial No. 1. Waung Sien Tsaung (汪憲章).
Arrested at 29, Lane 648, Ferry Road, the office of the Central Communications Department of the Chinese Communist Party. This accused when arrested stated that he was the husband of an amah who was in the house at the time, but next questioned this amah stated that the man was not known to her except as a resident of the house.

He is an associate of Serial Nos. 4 & 6 and believed to be a member of the Central Communications Department.

THE CHINA PRESS, WEDNESDAY, JULY 24, 1935

Big Red Gang
Believed In
Police Custody

Singapore Naval Base
Plans, Bank Balance
Found In Papers Seized

That the alleged Communist gang rounded up by Shanghai Municipal Police, working with the Bureau of Public Safety, on Monday night, had large financial resources at their command was revealed in the Second Kiangsu High Court yesterday morning when the suspects were brought up for trial.

In a raid conducted by detectives from the Hongkew Station, a bank book was seized, issued by a large local bank, showing that the deposits and withdrawals had been made regularly. The amounts dealt in, it was pointed out by the court prosecutor, were not small, but in thousands of dollars, indicating, it was stated, that the gang was operating in a big way and that its activities were widespread.

Naval Base Plans Found

Even more important was the fact that valuable papers and documents were seized during the raid, indicating that contacts were being maintained with Communist organizations in the Federated Strait Settlements and especially the city of Singapore. Plans of the Singapore Naval Base were found in possession of the suspects, as well as reams of correspondence between people in Malaya and the gang here.

That the gang was one of the most active and most important rounded up since the raids that followed the arrest of Paul and Gertrude Reugg four years ago was revealed by the fact that papers showing intimate knowledge of the activities of the Red Army in China were also seized. Although this important point was not brought out at yesterday's hearing of the suspects, THE CHINA PRESS received its information concerning the importance of some of the documents seized from reliable and official sources. Among the papers on the activities of the Red Army was a map showing movements of this force and the disposition of troops.

In all, a total of 24 suspects were haled before the court yesterday for preliminary hearing preparatory to their being handed over to the Bureau of Public Safety for trial in the Chinese courts. Seven of these were women.

Citywide Arrests Made

Five were taken into custody in raids by the Hongkew Police, while 11 were nabbed Monday evening by operatives from the Gordon Road Police Station. One was arrested on Moulmein Road, while another was nabbed on Jessfield Road. Central Police Station operatives made one arrest, taking a broker named Pan Yu-len, with offices at 205 Peking Road, into custody. Kiaochow Road police nabbed three, two women and one man, while two others were picked up on Chengtu Road and one on Taku Road.

Police were active from late afternoon until late at night, raids being conducted in all parts of the city. At the conclusion of activities

out of 25 sought had been arrested. All arrests were made on warrants issued by the First Special District Court, information concerning the activities of the accused being furnished by the Bureau of Public Safety.

One of the accused, a man giving his name as Lee Chien, left the court in something of quandry as to his possible connection with the case, as well as concerning his identity. In fact, he almost succeeded in making another "Mr. X" out of himself. He was one of the five picked up by Hongkew Station operatives and when taken into custody, immediately set up a claim of false arrest.

Innocence Claimed

He persisted with this claim when brought before the court yesterday morning and informed the judge that he had just arrived from Nanking when arrested, adding that he had no connection with the Communists, and therefore should be given his freedom at once.

A short, slight man of about 30 years of age, dressed in a grey suit of foreign-cut clothes, he monopolized the attention of the tribunal for several minutes. Asked where he lived, he stated that he had no address since he had just come to Shanghai a few hours before being arrested and had not managed to obtain lodgings.

Police, however, presented entirely contradictory evidence. Among other things, they questioned the man's story that he had just arrived from Nanking on the grounds that he had no luggage when arrested, not even a change of collars or shirts, and that, to them, appeared sufficient evidence that he was attempting to hide his real address from the authorities.

Tries To Destroy Ticket

In the first part of his story, the accused stated that he had never been in Shanghai before, but an examination of the suit of clothes he wore revealed the label of a Shanghai tailor. He also had an entrance ticket for a local park in his possession when nabbed and was caught in the act of trying to destroy it shortly after his arrest.

Asked to explain the label in his suit, the accused finally admitted that he had been in Shanghai before but that occasion was a long time ago. He had purchased the suit, then, he declared. The suit, however, appeared to be rather new and the prisoner's attention was called to this fact. He pointed out that he was careful with his clothes.

Despite the barrage of questions that were fired at him, the man stuck to his story, with the result that the court failed to learn the address that the police insisted existed. The hearings of all 24 concluded, the case was remanded sine die.

The suddenness of the raids Monday evening and the dispatch and efficiency with which they were carried out has left in doubt as to their importance. Whether there is any connection between the suspects arrested and Joseph Weber, better known as the "international Mr. X," however, is not known at present.

My name is Whaung Sien Tsaung, age 36, I am a native of
Anhwei. At present I live at 29 Ming Foh Li, Ferry Road;
I am married and my wife Whaung Tsang Sz, age 37, lives with me
at the above address where we work for Wen Sz Pao, a Tea Broker.
I was educated privately for some years but at the age of 15, I
went to a small school and continued my education there until I
was 18 years of age, in March of this year 1935, with my wife I
left Anhwei and together we came to Shanghai to look for work.
We both found employment with the afore mentioned Wen Sz Pao
living at the above address. He told me that he was a tea broker
but I do not know where he carries on his business. Before
living at the above address he told me that he had previously
lived in Tientsin Road Shanghai. My wife is amah for my
employers mistress and I am engaged in performing coolie work.
Yesterday July 21. at 10 a.m. my master and his mistress left
for Anhwei, they took a small box with them as luggage, he did
not tell me which town he was going to but said that he would
return after one month. At no time either before or after
coming to live in Shanghai have I been engaged in either
communistic or other political activities and I have never known
had any reason to think that my master has been engaged in
such activities. I have no friends or relatives in Shanghai
but I write to my parents in Anhwei and sometimes I receive
letters from them; I am not in communication with anyone in
Shanghai. My employer told me on one occasion that he had
lived in Shanghai for three or four years. Before my master left
he gave me $80 for expenses.

My name is Pan Yee Lu. I am 56 years of age and was born in Hwang Nei Hsien, Hupeh. I was educated in a private school in my native place for ten years and at the age of 17 was taken on as a junior teacher in a primary school. At the age of 25 I joined the Chinese Army in Wuchang under Tutai Li Yuan Hung as a private soldier. Two Years later I joined the military academy in Wuchang and two years later was appointed to the commissioned rank of captain. In 1909 I escaped to Japan to avoid arrest by the Manchu Authorities because of my activities in the Dang Hui Wei (a Kuomintang Organization). I studied military training in the Dah Sung Physical Training Academy, Tokio, for about one year. In July 1910 I returned to Wuchang and took part in the uprising against the Manchus started by Li Yuan Hung. In 1911 the Republic was established and I obtained employment in Peking as a Japanese interpreter. In 1913 I returned to Hupeh and took part in the revolution against Yuan Shi Kai in Hankow. I remained in hiding in Shanghai from 1913 to 1916 and then joined the staff of Li Yuan Hung in Peking. I was in Shanghai in 1917 and in 1918 was in Hupeh where I took part in the revolution against Tuan Chi Jui. During 1920 I participated in the revolt against Chen Chun Ming in Fukien and in 1924 went to Canton as staff officer to General Ho Chen Ching. During the same year I joined Sun Yat Sen's northern expedition but was forced to return to Canton owing to sickness. 1925 found me again in Shanghai and soon afterwards I returned to Hupeh to join

RECORD OF INVESTIGATION.

Summary of evidence against Chow Han Ping
(周漢平) and Lee Sieu Lay (李秀蘭).

On July 24, 1935 on the authority of a warrant issued at the request of the Public Safety Bureau detectives visited House 15, Lane 302, Yates Road, and there arrested Chow Han Ping and his wife, Lee Sieu Lay on a charge of being communists.

No literature or documents of an incriminating nature were found, but in a packet of cigarettes thrown on the floor by the male accused was found the attached document.
